tensions.name: Generic BSSA14 on rock vs Himalaya-specific basin-aware shaking

side_a.position: A standard global GMPE with a Vs30 term gives defensible first-order PGA for a public scenario tool.
side_a.evidence: Open GEM/BGS Nepal PGA grid uses generic models; BSSA14 sigma already computed in the Atlas.

side_b.position: Gorkha records show Himalaya-specific attenuation fits better and Kathmandu basin long-period amplification far exceeds code spectra.
side_b.evidence: KATNP spectra peaks ~0.4 s and ~5 s above code; Siddhitol >1 s exceeds NBC spectra.

tensions.resolution: Side A for the engine, Side B for the defaults. The defect that matters is the single 760 m/s rock default, not BSSA14 itself; a slope-based Vs30 grid plus visible sigma and a stated basin caveat fix most of the bias for PGA. Himalaya-specific GMPE claims are abstract-only, so a Gorkha ShakeMap/station test should come before any logic-tree change.

tensions.name: Constant wave speeds vs fast, growing cascade floods

side_a.position: A simple hydrograph moved at a few constant speeds is transparent and gives usable travel-time bounds.
side_a.evidence: Mergili 2020 Palcacocha travel bounds 36-70 min come from models; simple routing is all a static site can run.

side_b.position: Himalayan GLOF and debris cascades move far faster near the source and gain volume downstream, so constant 2-6 m/s with a fixed peak misleads.
side_b.evidence: Bhote Koshi 2026: ~52 m/s near source decaying to 6-7 m/s, Devghat peak 2,600 to 5,850 m3/s; Melamchi aggradation 5-20 m; Tsho Rolpa breach peaks vary 3x.

tensions.resolution: Side B on physics, Side A on what to build: keep the simple engine but add a fast, distance-decaying near-field speed, report an earliest-to-latest arrival window, drop any implied attenuation, and label the model as clear-water and single-source. Evidence for the speeds is two preprints of one event, so treat numbers as provisional and hindcast Melamchi/Bhote Koshi.

tensions.name: Official dangerous-lake list vs small unlisted lakes

side_a.position: Scenario origins should follow ICIMOD's assessed list of 21 Nepal PDGLs (47 regionally).
side_a.evidence: ICIMOD/UNDP 2020 ranks lakes on dam, glacier and surroundings criteria.

side_b.position: Recent destructive outbursts came from small or transboundary lakes on no list, and the list itself churns.
side_b.evidence: Thame 2024 two small lakes; Bhote Koshi from Tibet; only 13 of 21 PDGLs carried over from the 2011 list.

tensions.resolution: Side B: restricting origins to the list builds in a known blind spot. But expansion must be tiered and labelled (assessed / upstream of Nepal / unassessed) using the CC BY open HMA inventory, and shipped together with the framing safeguards in the next tension.

tensions.name: Forecasting success vs last-mile failure

side_a.position: Nepal's flood warning works: deaths fell from 166 (2017) to 27 (2022) after FFEWS and SMS.
side_a.evidence: WMO; Ncell 4.4 million SMS in 2023; BRCHP station and radar upgrades.

side_b.position: Warnings still fail at the last mile: unequal access, generic wording and no action guidance.
side_b.evidence: Sept 2024 accurate four-day alert yet ~250 deaths; 2026 Bhote Koshi generic Nepali-only SMS and 38.8 min alert after trigger; Budimir/Bhandari: barriers in access, understanding and ability to act.

tensions.resolution: Both, scoped: riverine forecast warnings improved; flash, urban, cascade and transboundary events still fail at dissemination. A daily static site cannot fix sub-hour latency, so the Atlas should invest in preparedness (place-specific arrival windows, printable plans) and in honest data age, not try to be a warning channel.

tensions.name: Plural unofficial maps: useful diversity or a source of contested authority

side_a.position: Diverse maps from several modellers encourage improvement through competition and fill gaps official maps leave.
side_a.evidence: Haughton & White note the benefit of diversity; Open Cities/KLL OSM mapping produced crisis maps used by the army in 2015.

side_b.position: Inconsistent hazard maps let people mobilise scientific uncertainty to dispute official maps; lines carry legal and financial weight.
side_b.evidence: Haughton & White: inconsistency in modelling created opportunity for challenge; Christchurch red-zone disputes.

tensions.resolution: Side B governs the Atlas's design: an unofficial site publishing scenario maps beside official data risks being read as a competing authority. Use no zone lines with legal-sounding names, cite official products, show where the Atlas differs and why, and seek written endorsement or partnership (KLL, ICIMOD, DHM) rather than standing alone.

tensions.name: Deterministic danger levels vs probabilistic forecasts

side_a.position: Simple threshold levels (warning, danger) are what people and officials act on.
side_a.evidence: DHM SMS and bulletins use colour-coded levels; stakeholders favoured colour codes.

side_b.position: Thresholds are hard to calibrate (false alarms vs misses); probabilistic forecasts add lead time (Karnali 2-3 h to 7-8 h) but are hard to convey.
side_b.evidence: Budimir/Bhandari analysis; NHESS community-based EWS study.

tensions.resolution: For the Atlas's live river data, show DHM's own threshold levels as the primary signal (do not invent new ones) and add trend and time-to-threshold context as secondary; reserve probability for scenario ranges, phrased as ranges not percentages, consistent with the natural-frequency caveat for rare events.
